issues.legal_issue: A deliberate positive assertion known to be false in an affidavit filed before a court can constitute criminal contempt by obstructing the administration of justice.
material_facts: An injunction restrained the respondents from dealing with specified immovable property without the court’s leave.
In an affidavit filed in connection with an application for clarification, the first respondent positively asserted that no property had been sold and that no steps had been taken to sell it.

Documentary evidence indicated that the property had been sold before the affidavit was made, although the Court did not determine the validity of the sale because that matter was pending in a civil court.
The Court found the affidavit’s statement to be a deliberate and fabricated falsehood, not merely a denial.
issues.conclusion: The respondents were guilty of contempt because the deliberate false statement in the affidavit interfered with or tended to obstruct the administration of justice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(c)(iii) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 includes conduct that interferes or tends to interfere with, or obstructs or tends to obstruct, the administration of justice. A deliberate positive assertion known to be false in a court affidavit is not to be treated as a mere denial. The Court distinguished Afzal v. State of Haryana, Rita Markand v. Surjit Singh Arora, and Secretary, Hailakandi Bar Association v. State of Assam on their facts, while relying on the purpose of contempt jurisdiction to protect the administration of justice and the authority of courts.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and court_affidavit_filed and positive_assertion_known_false and deliberate_falsehood

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A proceeding was brought before a court alleging contempt.
predicates.court_affidavit_filed: A person filed an affidavit before a court.
predicates.positive_assertion_known_false: The affidavit positively asserted a fact that its maker knew was false.
predicates.deliberate_falsehood: The false assertion was made deliberately rather than inadvertently.

issues.definition: When a contempt proceeding concerns a deliberately false positive assertion known to be false in an affidavit filed before a court, the rule treats the contemnor as guilty of criminal contempt.

issues.legal_issue: A court may impose punishment for contempt only when the conduct substantially interferes, or tends substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice, and an unconditional apology does not necessarily excuse such conduct.
material_facts: The Court found that the affidavit contained a deliberate falsehood, but the statement was made in an application for clarification after the transfer order had already been made.
The Court found no definite advantage had been gained through the statement and treated that circumstance as relevant to punishment, not to whether contempt had been committed.
The respondents tendered an unconditional apology.
The Court considered the false sworn statement sufficiently serious to warrant punishment and imposed a fine on each respondent.
issues.conclusion: The apology did not exonerate the respondents; the Court imposed a fine on each of them, with imprisonment in default of payment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 bars punishment unless the contempt substantially interferes, or tends substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice. Rachapudi Subba Rao v. Advocate General, Andhra Pradesh was cited on the scope of that requirement; Legal Remembrancer v. Martial Ghose and Attorney-General v. Times Newspapers Ltd. were cited for the distinction between technical contempt and conduct warranting punishment. Whether a contemnor gained an advantage is immaterial to commission of the offence but relevant to punishment. The Court held that an unconditional apology did not, in the circumstances, exonerate the respondents.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and contemnor_found_guilty and conduct_substantially_interfered_with_justice and unconditional_apology_tendered

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A proceeding was brought before a court alleging contempt.
predicates.contemnor_found_guilty: The court found the person guilty of contempt.
predicates.conduct_substantially_interfered_with_ju: The court found that the contempt substantially interfered, or tended substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice.
predicates.unconditional_apology_tendered: The person tendered an unconditional apology to the court.

issues.definition: Where a person found guilty in a contempt proceeding has substantially interfered with the due course of justice, tendering an unconditional apology does not prevent the rule from resulting in punishment by a fine.

issues.legal_issue: The Court declined to order an examination of documents by the Central Bureau of Investigation on the separate application before it.
material_facts: A separate application asked the Court to direct the Central Bureau of Investigation to examine documents.
The Court declined to make that direction and rejected the application without an order as to costs.
issues.conclusion: The application for a direction to the Central Bureau of Investigation to examine documents was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated no legal test or earlier authority for rejecting this application; it simply declined to pass the requested order.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A proceeding alleging contempt was before the Court.
predicates.ancillary_document_examination_request_m: An application requested that an investigative agency examine documents.

issues.definition: In a contempt proceeding, when an ancillary request is made for an investigative agency to examine documents, the rule records the Court’s rejection of that request.
